item.title: A first introduction to Matrix Product State algorithms for the integration of Lindblad equation
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Four matrix product state (MPS) extensions of TEBD integrate the 1D Lindblad equation: vectorized TEBD, positive-operator-preserving purification TEBD, quantum trajectories, and quantum state diffusion.

Grade 0.389 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Christophe Chatelain (LPCT)

Asks

How do standard MPS-based time-evolution algorithms compare in accuracy, positivity preservation, and computational cost when solving Lindbladian dynamics of 1D open quantum systems?

But

One-dimensional quantum lattice systems. Evaluated on an exactly solvable free fermion chain benchmark.

Tools

matrix product states (MPS) · time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) · vectorized master equation · quantum jump trajectories · quantum state diffusion

Abstract

In this introductory review, we present and compare four algorithms for the numerical integration of the Lindblad equation for one-dimensional quantum lattice systems. All four methods are based on Matrix Product State representations and can be viewed as extensions of the Time-Evolving Block Decimation (TEBD) algorithm to open quantum systems. Two approaches directly integrate the vectorized Lindblad equation, one of them explicitly enforcing the positivity of the density matrix. The other two rely on stochastic unravelings of the Lindblad equation, namely the quantum trajectory and quantum state diffusion approaches. We discuss the principles, numerical implementation, accuracy, and computational efficiency of the different methods, and benchmark them against an exactly solvable free fermion model.

item.title: Optical Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Surveys discrete- and continuous-variable optical quantum computing architectures, measurement-based cluster-state models, and non-universal algorithms (boson sampling, VQEs, QML).

Grade 0.381 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum simulations with ultracold quantum gases” · Hamza Hasnaoui, Leonardo Limongi, Taira Giordani, Beatrice Polacchi, Alberto Quaranta, Martino Bernard, Fabio Sciarrino, Mirko Lobino

Figure

Taxonomy mapping discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal optical quantum computing models alongside non-universal photonic applications.

Asks

How do optical encoding schemes and computing architectures compare across universal and non-universal quantum platforms?

But

Photonic scaling is constrained by weak single-photon nonlinearities, probabilistic gate generation, and optical propagation losses.

Tools

integrated photonics · continuous-variable squeeze states · discrete-variable cluster states · linear optical interferometry

Abstract

Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

item.title: Qurrium: A Python package for randomized measurement-based estimation of quantum state properties
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Presents Qurrium, a Qiskit-based Python library implementing classical shadow and Haar-measure randomized measurement protocols to estimate purity, second-order Rényi entropy, Pauli expectation values, and asymmetric unbiased state overlap fˆ2(ρ,ρ′).

Grade 0.379 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Huai-Chun Chang, Teik-Hui Lee, Arthur Strauss, Yu-Cheng Lin, Hsiu-Chuan Hsu

Figure

State overlap Tr(ρ(t)ρ(0)) versus dimensionless evolution time Jt under ZZ Ising dynamics using linear estimator fˆ1 and two-state estimator fˆ2, comparing ideal AerSimulator simulation, analytical theory, and superconducting QPU hardware data.

Asks

How can randomized measurement protocols like classical shadows be implemented in a native Python/Qiskit workflow for both end-to-end execution and standalone hardware data analysis?

But

Demonstrated on a two-qubit superconducting processor and noiseless 6-to-8 qubit circuit simulations; currently lacks integrated real-time end-to-end hardware execution.

Tools

Qurrium Python package · Qiskit AerSimulator · Classical shadow protocol · Superconducting QPU (Academia Sinica) · Quantum Machines OPX1000

Code. https://github.com/qurrium/qurrium

Abstract

Estimating quantum state properties is essential across a wide range of applications, from studying quantum many-body physics to benchmarking quantum hardware. We present Qurrium, a Python package built on Qiskit that implements randomized measurement protocols for estimating purity, second-order Rényi entropy, expectation values of Pauli observables, and state overlap. In this paper, we focus on the classical shadow protocol and demonstrate two workflows in Qurrium. One is the end-to-end workflow that integrates quantum circuit preparation, simulation, measurement, and analysis. The other is the standalone estimation workflow that accepts pre-collected measurement data from any hardware platform in Qurrium's data format. We demonstrate both workflows through examples of a cluster state and an Ising time-evolved state. Furthermore, we report results obtained from a superconducting quantum processor developed by Academia Sinica and analyzed using the standalone estimation workflow. Qurrium is built on Qiskit, the dominant framework in quantum computing software, making it directly accessible to the large community of researchers already working with Qiskit. The source code is openly available at https://github.com/qurrium/qurrium and the example code is provided at https://github.com/qurrium/classical-shadow-examples.

item.title: Fast Evaluation of the Sixth-Order Time-Convolutionless Master-Equation Generator and Beyond
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Evaluates the complete Hadamard-reduced sixth-order time-convolutionless master-equation generator time series in O(Ntlog2⁡Nt) operations and O(Nt) storage at fixed system dimension.

Grade 0.357 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Jiahao Chen, Sirui Chen, Dragomir Davidovic

Figure

Runtime scaling versus grid size Nt up to 225 points on one CPU core, showing the O(Ntlog2⁡Nt) scaling of the full TCL6 generator and isolated history kernels compared to direct integration.

Asks

How can the two remaining ordered integrals in the sixth-order time-convolutionless master-equation generator be evaluated faster than direct quadrature?

Before

Direct quadrature of the Hadamard-reduced TCL6 generator requires O(Nt3) operations at fixed system dimension.

But

Stationary centered Gaussian bath, finite-dimensional system, single Hermitian coupling operator, and dynamics within the perturbative TCL validity regime.

Tools

Hadamard reduction · exact dyadic recursion · 1D causal convolutions (FFT) · ordered time-gap coordinates

Code. https://github.com/jcarrots/fasttcl

Abstract

Direct quadrature of the Hadamard-reduced sixth-order time-convolutionless (TCL6) generator at all N_t sampled times requires O(N_t³) operations at fixed system dimension. We derive an exact reduction for a finite-dimensional system coupled through one Hermitian operator to a stationary centered Gaussian bath. By separating fixed operator coefficients from scalar bath kernels, the complete TCL6 time series is reduced to cumulative sums and first-order recurrences, one-dimensional causal convolutions, and an exact dyadic recursion for interlocked histories. With the algorithm, evaluating the complete TCL6 time series requires O(N_tlog² N_t) operations at fixed system dimension. In addition, we show that TCL2n can be evaluated with O(N_tlogⁿ⁻¹ N_t) complexity. A fixed finite Matsubara expansion of the bath correlation function permits O(N_tlogN_t) evaluation at any fixed TCL order. These reductions enable fast long-time simulations of non-Markovian open quantum systems within the regime of validity of the TCL expansion.

item.title: Collider Detector Observables from Lattice Spin Systems
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Formulation of lattice detector operators via continuity current jjE reproduces continuum energy-flow observables ℰ(nˆ) and matches 2d Ising CFT predictions at criticality.

Grade 0.344 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · João Barata, Ying-Ying Li, Bo Wang, Hua Xing Zhu

Figure

Scaling dimensions Δ versus spin s extracted via DMRG and Ritz methods on an N=24 lattice compared against exact CFT predictions (top); two-point correlator chord fits and stress-tensor Ward identity checks on N=48 (bottom).

Asks

Can asymptotic energy-flow detector observables be formulated and computed quantitatively on finite lattice spin systems?

But

Exploratory calculations on 1D spin chains (N=24,48 sites); results retain finite-bandwidth and packet-preparation systematic dependence.

Tools

DMRG · Time-Evolving Block Decimation (TEBD) · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Krylov subspace / Ritz states

Abstract

Detector observables pose a fundamental challenge for nonperturbative lattice methods due to their intrinsically real-time and asymptotic nature. We propose quantum simulation platforms as an ideal setting for studying these observables. Using quantum spin systems as a demonstration, we construct lattice detector operators and establish their connection to continuum energy-flow observables. We demonstrate this framework in the 1+1-dimensional quantum Ising model, where finite lattice calculations show quantitative agreement with conformal field theory expectations at criticality. These results support the interpretation of the lattice flow operators as regulated counterparts of continuum detectors in the scaling and asymptotic limits, providing a concrete route toward realizing high-energy collider physics on table-top quantum platforms.

item.title: Graph lattice sums and graph zeta functions for long-range interacting quantum lattice models
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Evaluates high-order graph lattice sums for long-range interacting quantum models deterministically, reducing compute times from tens of thousands of core-hours down to 10 minutes on a single core for a 10th-order series (7,136 graphs, up to 30-dimensional sums) on a 4,096-point 3D momentum grid.

Grade 0.341 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Andreas Alexander Buchheit, Andreas Rupp

Figure

Three-dimensional dispersion relation ω(𝒌,λ) across the Brillouin zone of a 3D long-range transverse-field Ising model on a cubic lattice at λ=−0.03 and power-law exponent ν=4, showing non-analytic behaviour at the Γ point.

Asks

How can the high-dimensional oscillatory graph lattice sums in linked-cluster perturbation theory of long-range interacting quantum lattice models be computed without stochastic Monte Carlo methods?

Before

Monte Carlo graph lattice sums required cluster-scale runtimes (typically a full day on a cluster per momentum evaluation) and suffered from stochastic error.

But

Monoatomic Bravais lattices; gapped quantum lattice models within the perturbative convergence radius.

Tools

Epstein zeta functions · graph block factorization and caching · series-parallel convolution algebra · tensor-network bucket elimination · fast Fourier transforms

Abstract

Taming the exponential increase of the Hilbert space dimension with system size in the simulation of gapped quantum lattice models is of the highest relevance for understanding and designing exotic quantum materials, where nonlocal interactions are of particular interest. High-order linked-cluster expansions provide access the solution of the eigenvalue problem for the infinite system, yet rely on the computation of high-dimensional oscillatory lattice sums with a graph structure, only approachable with Monte Carlo methods so far. This work resolves this issue, rendering all required graph lattice sums, referred to as graph zeta functions for kernels involving power-laws, computable. The resulting method reduces the evaluation time for state-of-the art series expansions from tenthousands of core-hours to minutes. After factorizing the lattice sum over blocks, each block is evaluated by the cheapest available strategy depending on its treewidth tw. Basic blocks admit analytic forms in terms of generalized zeta functions. Series-parallel blocks with tw≤2 can be computed at linear cost in the number of graph nodes and in the size of the momentum grid using a semi-analytical algebra based on Epstein zeta functions and rapidly decaying Fourier series. Finally, for tw>2, the method is combined with tensor-network bucket elimination yielding polynomial scaling of numerical work and memory in momentum grid size with exponents only growing with tw rather than with the number of vertices. Through use of FFT, the full momentum grid is recovered at the cost of a single momentum evaluation. We provide a detailed analysis of the precision and runtime of our method against analytic and numerical benchmarks. We further reproduce published Monte Carlo data for the transverse-field Ising model on different 1D, 2D, and 3D lattices, obtaining full agreement.

item.title: A Programmable Rydberg Quantum Bus for Nonlocal Connectivity
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Dispersive Rydberg atom chains act as coherent quantum buses to mediate effective quasi-all-to-all interactions between data units via virtual excitations, analytically derived using Green's-function continued fractions.

Grade 0.325 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · X. Jin, F. Yang, Weibin Li, X. Q. Shao

Figure

Population dynamics of data units coupled to a nine-atom Rydberg chain across single, double, and triple excitation manifolds, plotted against dimensionless time for V/J=40 and Δ/J=80.

Asks

Can a Rydberg atom array provide a stationary quantum bus to mediate coherent nonlocal connectivity between distant data units?

But

Off-resonant dispersive regime with Jμ≪mink⁡|Ek|; validated with Gaussian positional uncertainty σ=0.02 μm and Rydberg lifetimes up to T=77 K.

Tools

Green's function continued-fraction method · Feshbach partitioning · Monte Carlo wavefunction trajectories · Floquet engineering

Abstract

Scalable quantum networks require processing nodes with flexible internal connectivity, yet neutral-atom architectures remain constrained by the strong spatial dependence of native Rydberg interactions. Here we show that a Rydberg atom chain can act as a coherent quantum bus, converting a locally connected one-dimensional architecture into an effectively nonlocal interaction network. Virtual excitations in the dispersive regime mediate controllable interactions between spatially separated data units, which we derive analytically using a Green's-function continued-fraction method. The resulting mechanism is not restricted to single-excitation dynamics and supports several distinct functionalities, including Floquet-engineered chiral transport, remote entanglement of mechanical oscillators, and destructive interference for selectively suppressing unwanted dipole exchange. Simulations incorporating full long-range Rydberg interactions, atomic position fluctuations, and finite Rydberg-state lifetimes show that the mediated dynamics remain robust under experimentally relevant conditions. These results establish Rydberg chains as programmable coherent mediators for extending the internal connectivity of neutral-atom quantum nodes toward quasi-all-to-all coupling, providing a hardware-level route toward scalable and reconfigurable quantum-network architectures.

item.title: Quantum electrodynamics of equilibrium systems: A rigorous Maxwell-regularized functional-theoretic formulation
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Reformulates non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics as a density-functional theory over combined internal and external Maxwell sources, yielding a Moreau--Yosida regularized universal functional that removes the ultraviolet cutoff non-perturbatively via a Kohn--Sham construction.

Grade 0.324 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Markus Penz, Christian Jöns, Michael Ruggenthaler, Angel Rubio

Figure

Comparison between standard density-functional schemes (which treat external sources as fixed Hamiltonian parameters) and Maxwell-regularized functional theories (which incorporate field energy to combine internal observables with external sources into regularized mixed quantities).

Asks

How can equilibrium non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics be formulated non-perturbatively as an exact, mathematically regularized density-functional theory without unphysical representability issues and with the ultraviolet cutoff removed?

But

Equilibrium ground states in Coulomb gauge. Requires confining potentials (e.g. harmonic) or periodic boundaries to break translational invariance.

Tools

Maxwell duality · Moreau--Yosida regularization · Kohn--Sham auxiliary construction · Pauli--Fierz Hamiltonian · Vainberg--Bregman distance

Abstract

A framework for quantum electrodynamics of equilibrium systems is proposed that takes the Maxwell equations as foundational and links them to the structure of density-functional theory for the quantum system. By switching from purely internal observables like the one-particle density to combined internal and external quantities, the external sources and their energy are taken into account. A fully regularized functional theory emerges that avoids the usual representability problems. With the Kohn-Sham construction that links to an auxiliary uncoupled system, the ultra-violet cutoff can be removed and one arrives at a fully renormalized and non-perturbative light-matter description. Regularized forms of density-functional theory with and without magnetic fields appear as boundary cases, while the emergent physical picture reproduces the macroscopic Maxwell equations.
